day1.subject: operations across five offices
day1.body:
Marin, running operations across five offices in three countries is the point where scheduling stops being a conversation and starts being a spreadsheet nobody quite trusts. The part I would ask about is how long it takes to see that a job is going over before it has gone over, because most teams your size can report last month quickly and this week slowly.

Is that the shape of it, or have you already put something in place?

day15.subject: knowing this week rather than last month
day15.body:
Marin, one thing I did not ask about earlier. When a job starts slipping at Meridian, who notices first, and what are they looking at when they do. For most operations leads the answer is a person rather than a report, which works well until that person is on holiday or the job count doubles.

Worth a short conversation, or is this already handled?

day1.subject: twenty six people, five offices
day1.body:
Damir, twenty six people across five offices in three countries is a structure most agencies do not reach without deciding to. The question I would ask a founder running that is which of the five you can see clearly and which you take on trust, because the answer usually changes as the office count grows rather than as the headcount does.

Is that a fair reading, or does it look different from where you sit?

day15.subject: what you see and what you take on trust
day15.body:
Damir, a short follow-on thought. Founders running several offices tend to end up with one they know in detail and the rest reported to them monthly. That is a reasonable way to run it, and it is also the reason a bad quarter in one office is usually visible late rather than early.

Happy to leave it there if the timing is wrong.

day1.subject: five offices, one finance function
day1.body:
Ivana, you run finance across five offices in three countries, which is the point where month end stops being an afternoon and starts being a week. The part I would ask about is how long it takes to know which client work actually made money, because most teams that size can answer revenue quickly and margin slowly.

Is that the shape of it, or have you already solved it?

day15.subject: revenue quickly, margin slowly
day15.body:
Ivana, one more thought rather than a new question. In finance functions covering several offices the reporting usually arrives complete and late rather than partial and early, and the month that needed a decision has already closed by the time the numbers agree.

If that is not the problem at Meridian, that is a useful answer too.

day1.subject: a hundred and thirty eight people
day1.body:
Rowan, at a hundred and thirty eight people the revenue picture usually stops fitting in one head and starts living in several systems that disagree politely. The question I would put to a revenue lead is which number you would defend in a board meeting without checking it first.

Is that recognisable, or is Harbourline further along than that?

day15.subject: the number you would defend unchecked
day15.body:
Rowan, a short addition to my earlier thought. Revenue leaders at your size tend to trust the pipeline and question the margin, because the pipeline is one system and the margin is three. That is normal, and it is also why forecasting gets harder rather than easier as you grow.

Worth a conversation, or shall I leave it?

day1.subject: one number, several systems
day1.body:
Jesse, at a hundred and thirty eight people the interesting problem is usually not collecting the data but agreeing which copy of it counts. For a data product manager that tends to arrive as the same question from two teams with two different answers, neither of them wrong.

Is that the shape of it at Harbourline, or is the model already settled?

day15.subject: which copy of the number counts
day15.body:
Jesse, one more thought and then I will stop. Teams your size usually solve the pipeline before they solve the definitions, so the reports agree on the shape of the month and disagree on the total. It is a modelling problem rather than an engineering one, which is why it survives so many rebuilds.

Happy to leave this if it is not live for you.

day1.subject: forty people, founder in the numbers
day1.body:
Nikola, at forty people a co-founder is usually still the person who knows which projects are actually profitable, and that knowledge tends to live in one head rather than in a report. It works well, and it is also the thing that does not survive the next twenty hires.

Is that a fair description of Vantage, or have you handed it over?

day15.subject: what does not survive twenty more hires
day15.body:
Nikola, a brief addition rather than a new question. The founders I speak to at forty people are rarely short of information, they are short of a version of it somebody else can read. That is usually what makes the difference between delegating the work and delegating the judgement.

If the timing is wrong that is a fine answer.
